Question: How many different prime numbers are factors of \(N\) if \[ \log_2(\log_3(\log_5(\log_7N)))=11? \]
Solution:
Use the definition \(\log_b x=y\) if and only if \(x=b^y\). Removing the logarithms from outside inward gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_3(\log_5(\log_7N))&=2^{11},\\
\log_5(\log_7N)&=3^{2^{11}},\\
\log_7N&=5^{3^{2^{11}}},\\
N&=7^{5^{3^{2^{11}}}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All bases exceed \(1\), and the resulting logarithm arguments are positive, so these conversions respect the domains of the original logarithms.

The exponent \(5^{3^{2^{11}}}\) is a positive integer. Hence \(N\) is a positive integer power of \(7\). Since \(7\) is prime, its powers have no prime divisor other than \(7\). There is exactly \(1\) different prime factor, choice A.
